SEC17A-01.note: In 'not X but Y' the verb agrees with Y ('sweep', singular); active voice because 'the bat's path' is the object after the interrupter. B is attractive because 'ears' is the plural noun the reader meets first; C/D tempt readers who lose the object across the interrupting phrase.

SEC17A-02.note: 'Every X and every Y' takes a singular verb, and 'Since ... was written' requires the present perfect. A (plural compound reading) is the strong trap; B is singular but lacks the perfect.

SEC17A-03.note: Subject 'such a lens' is singular and is acted on, so singular passive. A is attractive after the long fronted modifier full of plurals (prisms, workshops, frames); C/D are active, which makes the lens the shipper.

SEC17A-04.note: 'That' takes the compound antecedent 'the skull and the lower jaw' (forced by 'their' and 'relative to each other'), so plural; past tense because the scene is past and the bones have since been removed. B is attractive by attaching 'that' to 'jaw' alone; C has the right number but wrong tense.

SEC17A-05.note: 'So + adjective + verb + subject ... that' inversion; the postposed subject 'measurements' is plural and the narrative is past ('ordered'). A is attractive because 'hall's' and the adjective look singular; B is plural but present.

SEC17A-06.note: 'As do' stands in for the action verbs 'hold back/release' with the plural postposed subject 'trumpets'. D ('as are') is attractive because the list of adjectives before 'trumpets' invites a linking verb; B is singular.

SEC17A-07.note: Fronted-predicate inversion; subject 'collapse' is singular, and 'to the present day' requires present perfect. A is singular but 'was once' implies the puzzle is over; B/C agree with the fronted 'specialists'.

SEC17A-08.note: The transposition precedes the past 'found', so past perfect. A (present perfect) is the attractive option; D's present tense for a dead compiler is strikeable on sight.

SEC17A-09.note: A long introductory 'Although' clause is joined to the main clause by a comma; semicolon and colon require an independent clause before them. A is attractive because the opening clause is long enough to feel complete.

SEC17A-10.note: Two independent clauses with the contrast adverb 'however' starting the second: semicolon before, comma after. C is attractive to readers who attach 'however' to the first clause, but there is no contrast there; D is a comma splice. B's colon-plus-however is never right.

SEC17B-01.note: 'The only one of the ... visitors that' takes a singular verb (antecedent 'one'), active because 'pollen' is the object after the interrupter. A (plural, agreeing with 'visitors') is the classic trap; B/C are passive.

SEC17B-02.note: In the cleft 'it is X that ...' the verb agrees with X ('shells', plural), and shells are misidentified, so passive. A is attractive because of 'it is'; C/D are active with shells doing the identifying.

SEC17B-03.note: Subject 'photoperiod' is singular, active because 'the week' is the object after the interrupter, present perfect for 'across those decades'. B is attractive through the plural 'decades' immediately before and the plural main subject; C/D are passive.

SEC17B-04.note: 'More than one core' takes a singular verb, and 'Until the team switched' marks a closed past span, so simple past. B is attractive because 'more than one' means several; D is singular but present perfect clashes with the finished period.

SEC17B-05.note: 'Not until ...' forces do-support inversion; subject 'eggs' is plural and the frame is present ('refill', 'hatch'). A is attractive because 'eggs' sits several words past the blank behind singular-looking adjectives; C is past.

SEC17B-06.note: Fronted-participle inversion; the subject 'account' is singular, and the scene is past (held, bore; it has since been moved). B agrees with the fronted 'envelopes'; A and C are singular but put the account in the box now.

SEC17B-07.note: 'Such + verb + subject ... that' inversion; the subject 'pressure' is singular, and 'ever since' with 'now survives' requires present perfect. B agrees with 'herds'; C is past perfect against a present result; D lacks the perfect required by 'ever since'.

SEC17B-08.note: The announcement uses the present perfect, and the clause 'once the chamber is refilled' is present, so the predicted outcome takes simple future. A is attractive as backshifted reported speech, but backshifting would need 'was refilled'.

SEC17B-09.note: The subject 'pigment' carries a restrictive reduced relative clause ('the illuminators ... ground ... lazuli'), so no punctuation separates it from the verb 'cost'. B is attractive because the long subject seems to need a pause; C's colon is strikeable.

SEC17B-10.note: A colon after an independent clause introduces the thing named ('one thing'). B is the strongest distractor: a comma would make 'a single heavy rain' read as an appositive to 'prices' or 'collapse'. A's semicolon fails because no independent clause follows; C is fused.

tells: Nearest-plural trap: in every agreement item where a plural noun sits right before the blank or is fronted (A-01 ears, A-03 frames, A-07 specialists, B-01 visitors, B-03 decades, B-06 envelopes, B-07 herds), the key is SINGULAR. Plural keys come only where the true subject is postposed or compound (A-04, A-05, A-06, B-02, B-05). A test-taker who learns 'the plural option agreeing with the nearby plural is the trap' clears most agreement items without finding the subject.

Cue word to present perfect: every item with 'since / ever since / across those decades / to the present day' has a perfect-aspect key (A-02, A-07, B-03, B-07). The adverb picks the tense without parsing.

2x2 number-by-voice option grids (A-01, B-01, B-02, B-03; A-03 nearly): the key is always the active option when an object noun follows the interrupter, and passive only when nothing follows (A-03, B-02). Spotting whether a bare noun phrase follows the interrupter settles voice mechanically.

In the agreement and tense items the key is never the option that adds an adverb shift or a different auxiliary (A-07 'was once', B-06 'has evidently been', B-07 'is now'). The odd-aspect option always loses.
Key letters are well spread (A:5, B:5, C:5, D:5), so there is no letter tell.

phase2_note: All 20 keys match my cold answers and every authored explanation produces its key and correctly dismisses each distractor. Nothing to drop per item: I found no disputed key, no failed exclusivity and no free elimination that wins outright. Weakest explanation: B-10's account of the comma option (it says rain becomes a third feared item). That is plausible but arguable, since some readers would take the comma as an appositive renaming 'one thing'; the key still stands. Batch-level concerns that are not per-item drop reasons: the nearest-plural-is-the-trap tell (7 singular keys against a fronted or adjacent plural) and the template pairs listed in summary.near_duplicates. Serving both members of a pair (e.g. A-05/B-07, A-07/B-06) in one form would let one item teach the other.
